clue.text: Hard to avoid astonishment if only wearing this?

definitions.text: Hard to avoid astonishment if only wearing this?

indicators.note: to avoid means the hard letter is kept out of the word for astonishment

parts.note: a shock is a sudden astonishment
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Someone appearing in nothing but one item of clothing would cause a stir.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a person wearing only a sock would cause astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: A sock is the single garment whose sole wearer would shock onlookers, so the clue describes it as a whole.

clue.text: Head of Physics in school dozes? It's the drink

indicators.note: in means the leading letter sits inside the dozes word

parts.note: naps are short sleeps, so dozes

indicators.note: Head of picks out the first letter of Physics

explanation.surface: A physics teacher nodding off at school is blamed on the booze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Physics' suggests a school department chief, but it is just the letter P.
explanation.definitionFit: Schnapps is a strong spirit, an example of an alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Plan a lot of time off in cathedral city

parts.note: a chart is a plan or map

indicators.note: a lot of means most but not all of the time-off word is used, losing its last letter

parts.note: rest is time off work

explanation.surface: Someone plans a long holiday in a city with a great church.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartres in northern France is famous for its Gothic cathedral, an example of such a city.

clue.text: Explains clue — unravelling is about time

indicators.note: unravelling means the letters of clue are untangled and set in a new order
about means the word is goes round the word for time

parts.note: a date is a point in time

explanation.surface: A setter explains how a clue comes apart, with timing involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clue' sits in the surface as the thing being explained, but it is anagram fodder; 'about' is a container, not 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: To elucidate something is to make it clear, a direct synonym of explaining it.

clue.text: Rugby team, note, covered in dirt? Just the reverse

indicators.note: covered in, swapped by the reverse, means the dirt word holds the note letter
Just the reverse says both that the dirt word is turned backwards and that the container order is swapped

parts.note: soil is earth or dirt
N is short for note, as in the note abbreviation used for a banknote

explanation.surface: A rugby side ends up covered in mud, or the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just the reverse' does double duty: SOIL is turned to LIOS, and the dirt covers the note rather than the note the dirt. The Lions are the British and Irish touring rugby team.
explanation.definitionFit: The British and Irish Lions are a famous touring rugby union side, so a rugby team.

clue.text: One may have grounds to show if one's drunk

definitions.text: One may have grounds to show if one's drunk

parts.words: One may have grounds to show if one's drunk
parts.note: sounds like an argument about drunkenness, but describes a vessel left with coffee dregs after its contents are drunk

explanation.surface: Someone may be able to justify showing they have been drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grounds' means coffee dregs, not reasons; 'one's drunk' means its contents are drunk, not a tipsy person.
explanation.definitionFit: After the drink is finished, a mug of brewed coffee may hold leftover grounds at the bottom.

clue.text: No criteria out of place following director with fixed opinions

indicators.note: following means the rearranged letters come after the director letter
out of place means the letters of the phrase are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A director with no rules who has stubborn views.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctrinaire person applies theory rigidly, so is dogmatic and holds inflexible views.

clue.text: Non-drinker suppresses his, swallowing water ultimately!

definitions.text: Non-drinker suppresses his, swallowing water ultimately!

indicators.note: suppresses means the teetotal letters press down round the rest

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, a non-drinker

indicators.note: swallowing means the word his takes in a letter

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately picks the last letter of water

explanation.surface: A teetotaller keeps their craving in check, finally drinking just water.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a teetotaller holds down the urge to drink and ends up gulping water.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong craving for drink is what a non-drinker must hold back, and water finally quenches it.

clue.text: Crime supported by evil sailor

indicators.note: in a down clue, supported by means the crime word sits on top of the next

parts.note: a sin is a wrongdoing or crime
bad means evil

explanation.surface: Wrongdoing backed by a wicked mariner.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinbad is the seafarer of the Arabian Nights tales, an example of a famous sailor.

clue.text: Hard to take in an increased level of attention

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
to take in food is to eat it

explanation.surface: Someone finds it difficult to absorb a raised level of focus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take in' looks like 'absorb', but here it means consume food.
explanation.definitionFit: When the heat is on, someone is under intense scrutiny or pressure, an idiomatic sense of raised attention.

clue.text: No new dispute after cancelling library's core book classification

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: after cancelling means the dispute word has a letter removed from it

parts.note: friction is conflict or disagreement

indicators.note: core points to the central letter of the word library

explanation.surface: A librarian, no longer quarrelling, sorts out how books are classified.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'core' of LIBRARY's seven letters is its middle R, removed from FRICTION to leave FICTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Libraries divide their stock into fiction and factual works, the latter being a standard category of books.

clue.text: 'Goddess' is a term abused

indicators.note: abused means the letters of the phrase are mistreated into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the word goddess has been misused.
explanation.definitionFit: Artemis is the Greek goddess of hunting and the moon, an example of a deity.

clue.text: Gin in Thermos?

parts.note: ruin the letters of mothers and they become the word Thermos, so the answer read as wordplay leads to this word

explanation.surface: Someone has hidden spirits in a vacuum flask.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer read as instructions, a word plus an anagram indicator, produces the clue's last word. Gin's nickname is old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: In old British slang, the spirit was nicknamed for its ruinous effect on families, especially mothers.

clue.text: Recalled article I regret about a Southern part of the globe

indicators.note: about means the turned pieces go round the next pair
recalled means the pieces are called back, read from right to left

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
taken as written
to rue is to regret

explanation.surface: A writer looks back on a piece they regret concerning the south of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled' turns A + I + RUE into EURIA; 'about' places AS inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurasia is the combined landmass of Europe and Asia, a large region of the world.

clue.text: Hispanic King limited by curious precaution

indicators.note: limited by means the king letter is hemmed in by the rearranged letters
curious means odd, so the letters of precaution are set in an odd order

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A Spanish-speaking monarch is hemmed in by some strange safety measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curious' reworks PRECAUTION; R goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Caribbean island Puerto Rico is Spanish-speaking, so is an example of a Hispanic person.

clue.text: List includes revolutionary romantic hero

indicators.note: includes means the list word holds the revolutionary inside it

parts.note: a roster is a list of names on duty
Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary

explanation.surface: A list of names features a rebel as a romantic lead.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Rochester is the brooding love interest in Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre, an example of a romantic hero.

clue.text: American bananas not for public consumption

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild into a new order

explanation.surface: Fruit from the US is kept off the market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like fruit but means mad, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Proceedings held privately, especially in court, are hidden from the public and its scrutiny.

clue.text: Down with horseplay ending in stark panic

parts.note: blue means down, as in feeling low
horseplay is boisterous fun

indicators.note: ending in picks out the last letter of stark

explanation.surface: Feeling low, a joker's rough games end in sheer terror.
explanation.definitionFit: A blue funk is a state of terror or great fear, an informal idiom for panic.

clue.text: Superior beer running short after one's working behind bar

indicators.note: behind means the following pieces come after the word for bar
after means the shortened beer comes at the end

parts.note: bar as a preposition means except, as in all bar one
one is I, the Roman numeral; the 's is is, a link
on means working, as a machine that is on

indicators.note: running short means the beer word loses its final letter

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A pub drinker's superior pint is running low while they work behind the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' is not a pub counter but 'except'; 'running short' cuts ALE to AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exceptional stands above the ordinary, so it is superior in quality.

clue.text: Wary, being upset over excluded juveniles

indicators.note: over means the turned letters go over and round the excluded word
being upset means the wary word is turned upside down, read backwards in a down clue

parts.note: shy means wary or cautious
out means excluded, as someone left out

explanation.surface: Cautious people are upset about young people being left out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being upset' suits a down clue, where the letters are turned upside down to read YHS; 'over' means wrapped round, not above.
explanation.definitionFit: Youths are young people in their teens, synonymous with juveniles.

clue.text: Shed's thin roof not quite finished

parts.note: lean means thin

indicators.note: not quite finished means the roof word lacks its last letter

parts.note: the top of a building is its roof

explanation.surface: A shed's flimsy roof has not been completed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed's' is the definition plus 'is' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A lean-to is a simple shelter built against a wall, a kind of shed.

clue.text: Several deliveries appear short — what should captain do?

parts.note: in cricket a set of six balls bowled in turn makes up one over

indicators.note: short means the appear word loses its last letter

parts.note: to seem is to appear

explanation.surface: A cricket captain worries that the bowling is falling short.
explanation.walkthrough: Overs are sets of six balls in cricket, a British sport; a captain directs the team.
explanation.definitionFit: A captain's job is to supervise the team or crew, the duty asked about in the question.

clue.text: English militiaman finally invested in quality explosive

indicators.note: invested in means these letters are placed inside the quality word

parts.note: a grade is a level of quality

indicators.note: finally picks out the last letter of militiaman

explanation.surface: An English soldier of a local force has put money into a fine explosive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invested in' reads like finance but means placed inside: EN goes into GRADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A grenade is a small bomb thrown by hand, an example of an explosive device.

clue.text: Reckon visitors will take time out

indicators.note: take, paired with out later in the clue, means the visitors word has a letter removed
out completes take out, so the time letter is removed from the visitors word

parts.note: guests are visitors

explanation.surface: Someone supposes their guests will take a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take time out' reads as a rest; split it into 'take ... out' around T.
explanation.definitionFit: To reckon is to suppose or estimate, a synonym of making a guess.

clue.text: Get on with endless duties, unfortunately unable to speak

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone awry, so the letters are mixed up
endless means the word duties loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A worker told to carry on with chores is, sadly, left speechless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims DUTIES to DUTIE, mixed with GETON by 'unfortunately'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tongue-tied means being too shy or flustered to talk, an idiom for speechlessness.

clue.text: Some proper upbringing, in the country

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A good rural childhood is described.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'in', which is a link word: 'in the country' cannot stand for the answer, 'the country' can.
explanation.definitionFit: Peru is a nation on the Pacific coast of South America, an example of a country.

clue.text: No promises to arrange bird-watching?

indicators.note: to arrange means the letters of the phrase are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: No guarantees can be made about organising a birding trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of 'word-batching' gives 'bird-watching', so the definition is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A transposition of initial sounds can turn a phrase like word-batching into another, illustrating the device by example.

clue.text: Likely to hum a line

definitions.meaning: in British slang to hum is to smell bad, so this means foul-smelling
a row of soldiers standing side by side

explanation.surface: Someone is apt to sing a phrase of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hum' is British slang for giving off a bad smell, not singing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means foul-smelling as an adjective and a row of soldiers as a noun.
